title: LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters
goal: By the end you can explain why an LSM tree turns random writes into sequential ones, trace a write, a flush, a read and a compaction through a memtable, SSTables and Bloom filters, size a Bloom filter, and build a small LSM store.

warmup.q: A key-value store keeps its data in 6 sorted, immutable files on disk plus a sorted buffer in memory. You look up a key that is in none of them. How many of the 6 files does the lookup usually read from disk?
options: All 6, because the key could be in any of them
1, because the newest file has an entry for every key
About 3, because it binary-searches across the files
Usually none: a small in-memory filter per file rules most of them out
warmup.why: Each file has a Bloom filter in memory. For a key that was never added, a filter at 10 bits per key says "maybe" only about 1% of the time, so the lookup almost never touches the disk. Without filters it would read a block from all 6 files. Files are separate sorted runs, so there is no binary search across them, and the newest file only holds recent writes.

sections.h: A B+tree pays for every random insert with a whole page
sections.body:
Lesson 4's B+tree changes data in place. To insert a key, it finds the leaf where the key belongs, changes that page in memory, and later writes the whole 8 KB page back. When keys arrive in order, they all land on the rightmost leaf, and one page absorbs hundreds of inserts before it is written. When keys are random, such as card fingerprints, idempotency keys or `gen_random_uuid()` ids, every insert lands on a different leaf.

The Try it measures that on a PostgreSQL table with a million rows and a UUID primary key. 10,000 inserts with time-ordered keys dirty 105 pages and write 1.5 MB to the write-ahead log. 10,000 inserts with random keys dirty 4,278 pages and write 26.5 MB, because the first change to each page after a checkpoint (lesson 1: the point by which all earlier changes have reached the table files) also copies the whole page into the log. Lesson 6 explains why. The rows hold 24 bytes of data each, 240 KB in all. That is a write amplification (bytes written per byte stored, lesson 1) of over 100, and the 4,278 dirty pages still have to go back to disk later, about 33 MB of 8 KB writes.

Version 1 is lesson 1's log: append every write to the end of one file. Every write is sequential and cheap. But the file has no order, so reads need a hash map of every key in RAM, and range queries are out.

Version 2 keeps cheap writes and gets order back by sorting in memory first. New writes go into a **memtable**, a sorted map in RAM: a `TreeMap` in your lab, a skip list in RocksDB. Writing to it costs no disk I/O. When it reaches a size limit (64 MB by default in RocksDB), the whole memtable is written out in key order as one file, a sorted string table or **SSTable**, a name from Google's Bigtable paper (2006). That is one sequential write of 64 MB where a B+tree would have done thousands of scattered page writes. Then the memtable starts empty.

An SSTable never changes after it is written. An update puts a newer version into the memtable, which later lands in a newer SSTable. A delete writes a tombstone, the same marker as lesson 1. So the disk holds a growing stack of files, newest on top, and older files may still hold stale versions of a key.

That design is the **log-structured merge tree**, or LSM tree, described by Patrick O'Neil and three colleagues in 1996. RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB and CockroachDB's Pebble are LSM trees. The figure is the picture for this lesson: a memtable in RAM, a stack of SSTables on disk, and a write-ahead log beside them, because the memtable lives in memory and a crash would wipe it.

try.title: Count what random keys cost a B+tree
steps: From `labs/`, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait` and open psql with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.
Create two tables with a UUID primary key and a million rows each: one filled with time-ordered `uuidv7()` ids, one with random `gen_random_uuid()` ids. The inserts take several seconds.
After a CHECKPOINT, insert 10,000 more rows into each and read the `Buffers` and `WAL` lines. Predict which insert writes more log, and by how much.
Stop PostgreSQL before the next Try it, which needs memory for Cassandra: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v`.

```text
...
```

(output trimmed). Both inserts write about 20,000 log records: one per row and one per index entry. Time-ordered keys go to the rightmost leaf, so 10,000 rows dirty 105 pages and take 3 full-page images (`fpi`). Random keys spread over a 4,800-page index: 4,278 dirty pages, 4,190 full-page images, 17 times the log volume. `dirtied` counts pages that now differ from disk and must be written back later. Your counts differ a little, but not the ratio.

sections.h: An SSTable is a sorted file, and a read goes from the newest file to the oldest
sections.body:
Inside, an SSTable is records in key order: key length, key, value length, value, as in your lab. The records are grouped into blocks (4 KB by default in RocksDB; 16 records in your lab). Because the file is sorted, you don't need an index entry for every key. A **sparse index** holds only the first key of each block and where the block starts. To find `auth:00500`, binary-search the index for the last block whose first key is not above it, read that one block, and scan it. In your lab, 1,000 records need 63 index entries, and a lookup costs exactly one read. The index is small, so the database keeps it in memory. RocksDB loads it, with the Bloom filter of the next section, when it opens a table file.

Now the harder question: which file holds the key? A key can be in the memtable and in any number of SSTables, and only the newest version is right. So a read looks in the memtable first, then in the SSTables from newest to oldest, and stops at the first one that knows the key. If that first hit is a tombstone, the answer is "not found", and the older files must not be asked. The stepper runs this with two files and one tombstone.

The cost shows up for keys that aren't in the newest files. A key that only the oldest of 20 SSTables holds costs 19 useless block reads first, and a key that exists nowhere costs 20. Disk reads per lookup is **read amplification**, and an LSM tree has a lot of it unless it fights back. It does in two ways: a Bloom filter per file, which lets most useless reads skip the disk entirely, and compaction, which keeps the number of files down. The next two sections take them in turn.

Cassandra, in the Try it, is an LSM tree you can watch at work, and two details differ from your lab. Cassandra stores each column as a separate cell with its own timestamp, so an SSTable may hold only some columns of a row, and a read can need several files to rebuild one row: the trace for id 7 merges two. And Cassandra sorts each file by a hash of the partition key, not by the key itself, so neighbouring ids are not neighbours on disk.

stepper.title: Write, flush, read, compact
stepper.intro: Three authorizations, an update, a delete, three reads and one compaction. Use Next and Back, or the arrow keys.

frames.say: Three authorizations arrive: `put(auth:1, PENDING)` and two more. Each one is inserted into the memtable, a sorted map in memory, and appended to the WAL so a crash can't lose it. No data page is read or written.

Then the memtable starts empty.</text></svg>
frames.say: The memtable reached its size limit, so it is **flushed**: written to a new file in key order, in one sequential write, with a Bloom filter and a sparse index built on the way. That file is SSTable 1. It is immutable: nothing will ever change it in place.

Files are never edited.</text></svg>
frames.say: The capture for `auth:2` and a delete of `auth:3` arrive. SSTable 1 is not touched: the new value goes into the memtable, and the delete is stored as a **tombstone**, a marker that says "deleted as of now". SSTable 1 still holds the old values.

Two versions of auth:2 and auth:3 are on disk now,</text><text class="t-s" x="20" y="244" text-anchor="start">and the newer table must win.</text></svg>
frames.say: Another flush makes SSTable 2. Now the disk holds two versions of `auth:2` and two of `auth:3`. Nothing says which is current except the order of the files: SSTable 2 is newer, so its versions win.

Found CAPTURED.</text><text class="t-s" x="20" y="244" text-anchor="start">Stop at the first hit: SSTable 1 is never read.</text></svg>
frames.say: `get(auth:2)` checks the memtable first, then the tables from newest to oldest. SSTable 2's Bloom filter says "maybe", its index points at one block, and the block holds `CAPTURED`. The read stops at the first hit, so the stale `PENDING` in SSTable 1 is never read.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 258" role="img" aria-label="get(auth:1) skips SSTable 2 thanks to its Bloom filter and finds the value in SSTable 1."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="150" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="120.0" y="64" text-anchor="middle">memtable (RAM)</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="120.0" y="176" text-anchor="middle">no auth:1 here</text><rect class="box-ok" x="250" y="40" width="200" height="150" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="350.0" y="64" text-anchor="middle">SSTable 2 (newer)</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="266" y="96" text-anchor="start">auth:2 = CAPTURED</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="266" y="120" text-anchor="start">auth:3 = tombstone</text><text class="t-s t-ok" x="350.0" y="176" text-anchor="middle">filter: no. skip, 0 reads</text><rect class="box-a" x="470" y="40" width="190" height="150" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="565.0" y="64" text-anchor="middle">SSTable 1 (older)</text><text class="t-s t-code t-a" x="486" y="96" text-anchor="start">auth:1 = PENDING</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="486" y="120" text-anchor="start">auth:2 = PENDING</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="486" y="144" text-anchor="start">auth:3 = PENDING</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="565.0" y="176" text-anchor="middle">filter: maybe. found</text><text class="t-s" x="20" y="222" text-anchor="start">get(auth:1): SSTable 2's Bloom filter says no, so it costs no disk read.</text><text class="t-s" x="20" y="244" text-anchor="start">SSTable 1's filter says maybe, and its block holds PENDING.</text></svg>
frames.say: `get(auth:1)` is not in SSTable 2. Without help it would cost a block read to find that out. SSTable 2's **Bloom filter**, kept in memory, says "definitely not here", so the read skips the file without touching the disk and moves on to SSTable 1, which has it.

frames.say: `get(auth:3)` finds the tombstone in SSTable 2 and answers "not found" at once. If it carried on to SSTable 1, the deleted authorization would come back. A tombstone is a value that means "stop looking".

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 258" role="img" aria-label="Compaction merged SSTables 1 and 2 into SSTable 3, without auth:3."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="200" height="150" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="120.0" y="64" text-anchor="middle">memtable (RAM)</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="120.0" y="176" text-anchor="middle">empty</text><rect class="box-ok" x="250" y="40" width="200" height="150" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="350.0" y="64" text-anchor="middle">SSTable 3 (merged)</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="266" y="96" text-anchor="start">auth:1 = PENDING</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="266" y="120" text-anchor="start">auth:2 = CAPTURED</text><text class="t-s t-ok" x="350.0" y="176" text-anchor="middle">1 file, newest versions only</text><rect class="box-dim" x="470" y="40" width="190" height="150" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="565.0" y="64" text-anchor="middle">SSTables 1 and 2</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="565.0" y="176" text-anchor="middle">deleted after the merge</text><text class="t-s" x="20" y="222" text-anchor="start">compaction: merge both tables in key order, keep the newest version of each key,</text><text class="t-s" x="20" y="244" text-anchor="start">drop the tombstone and what it hid, then delete the inputs.</text></svg>
frames.say: **Compaction** merges the two files like the merge step of merge sort: read both in key order, keep the newest version of each key, write SSTable 3, then delete the inputs. The tombstone can go too, because no older file is left that could still hold `auth:3`. Reads now check one file instead of two.

try.title: Watch Cassandra flush and read
steps: From `labs/`, start Cassandra with `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml up -d --wait` (it takes about a minute), then open a shell in it: `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra bash`.
Create a table, write 1,000 rows and check the memtable and the SSTable count. Predict both numbers before and after `nodetool flush`.
List the new SSTable's files. Then update 100 rows, flush again and trace two reads: id 7 (updated) and id 700 (not updated). Predict which SSTables each read touches.

code.title: a shell in the Cassandra container
code.src:
cqlsh -e "CREATE KEYSPACE lsm WITH replication = {'class': 'SimpleStrategy', 'replication_factor': 1};
          CREATE TABLE lsm.auths (id int PRIMARY KEY, status text);"
for i in $(seq 1 1000); do echo "INSERT INTO lsm.auths (id, status) VALUES ($i, 'AUTHORIZED');"; done > /tmp/load.cql
cqlsh -f /tmp/load.cql
nodetool tablestats lsm.auths | grep -E 'SSTable count|Memtable cell count'
nodetool flush lsm auths
nodetool tablestats lsm.auths | grep -E 'SSTable count|Memtable cell count'
ls /var/lib/cassandra/data/lsm/auths-*/

for i in $(seq 1 100); do echo "UPDATE lsm.auths SET status = 'CAPTURED' WHERE id = $i;"; done > /tmp/upd.cql
cqlsh -f /tmp/upd.cql
nodetool flush lsm auths
cqlsh -e "TRACING ON; SELECT * FROM lsm.auths WHERE id = 7; SELECT * FROM lsm.auths WHERE id = 700;" \
  | grep -E 'Merging|Bloom|Partition index|live rows'

try.expect:
Before the flush all 1,000 rows are in the memtable and there is no SSTable. After it, one SSTable is on disk as a set of files:


sections.h: A Bloom filter says "definitely not here" with about 10 bits per key
sections.body:
A read wants to skip every SSTable that doesn't hold the key, without reading it. Version 1 keeps the set of every file's keys in memory. That is lesson 1's keydir problem again: 200 million keys of 40 bytes is 8 GB of RAM.

Version 2 gives up exact answers. Keep an array of m bits, all 0, and one hash function. To add a key, set the bit at `hash(key) mod m`. To check a key, look at its bit. A 0 means no key that hashes there was ever added, so the key is certainly absent and the file can be skipped. A 1 means "maybe": this key was added, or another key with the same bit was. With 10 bits per key, about 1 bit in 10 is set, so about 1 absent key in 10 gets a wrong "maybe", a **false positive**. A false positive costs one wasted block read. A wrong "no" would hide data, and this structure never gives one.

Version 3 is the **Bloom filter** (Burton Bloom, 1970): k hash functions instead of one. Adding a key sets k bits, and a key is "maybe present" only if all k of its bits are 1. More hashes set more bits, but an absent key must now match k bits by chance instead of one. For n keys in m bits the false-positive rate is about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, which is lowest when k is about 0.69 times the bits per key. At 10 bits per key that gives k = 7 and a rate of 0.82%. The figure shows a tiny filter giving both answers.

The cost is small and predictable, which is why every SSTable gets one. RocksDB's documentation gives 1% at 9.9 bits per key and 0.1% at 15.5. Cassandra's default `bloom_filter_fp_chance` is 0.01, and in the previous Try it its filter for 1,000 keys took 1,264 bytes, about 10 bits per key. A filter is built once, when its file is written. You can't remove a key from a Bloom filter, but an immutable file never needs to.

Bloom filters have one hard limit: they answer "is this exact key here?" and nothing else. A range query such as "every authorization for card 4242 today" can't use them, so it must open every file whose key range overlaps the range.

try.title: Measure false positives
steps: Predict: at 10 bits per key, what share of keys that were never added get a "maybe"?
From `labs/`, run the demo. It fills filters of 2 to 16 bits per key with 100,000 payment ids and probes each with 1,000,000 ids it never saw.
Run it again with ten times the keys: add `-Pargs=1000000`. Predict whether the rates change.
try.expect:
```text
bits/key  hashes  filter size  measured FP  formula
       2       1      24.4 KB       39.24%   39.35%
       4       3      48.8 KB       14.74%   14.69%
       6       4      73.2 KB        5.62%    5.61%
       8       6      97.7 KB        2.16%    2.16%
      10       7     122.1 KB        0.81%    0.82%
      12       8     146.5 KB        0.31%    0.31%
      16      11     195.3 KB        0.04%    0.05%
```

The measured rate matches the formula to a few hundredths of a percent. Every 2 extra bits per key cut the false positives by about 2.5 times, so 10 bits buy 1% and 16 bits 0.05%. With 1,000,000 keys every filter is 10 times bigger and the rates stay the same (0.82% at 10 bits per key in our run): the rate depends on bits per key, not on how many keys there are.

sections.h: Compaction merges files, and every design picks which cost to pay
sections.body:
Without compaction, files pile up. Every flush adds one, reads check more of them, and every overwritten value and deleted key keeps taking disk space. Disk bytes per byte of live data is **space amplification**; lesson 1's log reached 100 before a merge.

Compaction is the merge step of merge sort. Read several SSTables in key order at the same time, keep only the newest version of each key, write the result as new SSTables, then delete the inputs. A tombstone can be dropped only when no older file could still hold its key; drop it any earlier and the old value comes back. The stepper's last frame and your lab's `compact` merge everything into one file, so they can drop every tombstone.

Real stores merge a few files at a time, and how they pick them is the main tuning choice of an LSM tree.

Leveled compaction is RocksDB's default. Flushed files go into level 0, where their key ranges overlap. When level 0 has 4 files, they are merged into level 1. Each level below 0 is one sorted run (every key at most once, in order), cut into files of 64 MB by default whose key ranges don't overlap, and each level is about 10 times bigger than the one above. A read checks the level-0 files, then at most one file per level. The price is writing: a key is rewritten each time it moves down a level, and merging into a level 10 times bigger rewrites overlapping files there as well. RocksDB's wiki says leveled compaction's write amplification is often larger than 10.

Size-tiered compaction, Cassandra's default, waits for 4 files of similar size and merges them into one bigger file. Each byte is rewritten far fewer times, but a key can sit in many files, so reads check more of them, and a merge needs free disk space for its whole output.

You can't have it all. The RUM conjecture (Athanassoulis and colleagues, 2016) says a storage structure can bound two of read, update and memory overhead, and pays with the third. A B+tree reads in 3 or 4 pages but writes a page per random insert. An LSM tree writes sequentially but reads through several files and keeps stale versions until compaction. For a ledger queried by date ranges, pick the B+tree. For a flood of random-key writes read back by key, such as idempotency keys or a Kafka Streams state store, pick the LSM tree.

One Cassandra detail shows up in the Try it: compaction keeps a tombstone for `gc_grace_seconds`, 10 days by default, even when it could drop it. Another replica may have missed the delete, and without the tombstone a repair would copy the old row back from it. Cassandra's docs call a deleted row that returns this way a zombie.

try.title: Follow a tombstone through a compaction
steps: In the Cassandra shell from the earlier Try it, delete id 500 and flush. Predict what the new SSTable holds for it.
Run `nodetool compact` to merge every SSTable of the table, then dump partition 500 from the result. Predict: is the tombstone gone?
When you are done with this lesson, leave the shell and stop Cassandra from `labs/`: `docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml down -v`.

code.title: a shell in the Cassandra container
code.src:
cqlsh -e "DELETE FROM lsm.auths WHERE id = 500;"
nodetool flush lsm auths
cd /var/lib/cassandra/data/lsm/auths-*/
ls *Data.db
/opt/cassandra/tools/bin/sstabledump nb-3-big-Data.db -k 500

ls *Data.db
/opt/cassandra/tools/bin/sstabledump nb-4-big-Data.db -k 500 | grep -E 'key|deletion_info'

The delete becomes a third SSTable that holds only a tombstone for partition 500:

```text
nb-1-big-Data.db
nb-2-big-Data.db
nb-3-big-Data.db
[
  {
    "table kind" : "REGULAR",
    "partition" : {
      "key" : [ "500" ],

    },
```

After the compaction one file is left, and it still carries the tombstone:

```text
nb-4-big-Data.db

      "deletion_info" : { "marked_deleted" : "2026-11-07T18:45:42.347404Z", "local_delete_time" : "2026-11-07T18:45:42Z" }
```

The three files were merged into `nb-4`, newest version per partition, but the tombstone stays until `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days) has passed. The SELECT returns 0 rows. Your timestamps differ.

refs.title: Athanassoulis et al.: Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture (EDBT 2016)

analogy: An LSM tree works like a busy accounts office that never edits a ledger once it is bound. New entries go onto a notepad kept sorted by account number. When the notepad is full, a clerk copies it out clean into a new booklet and shelves it, newest on the left. To answer "what is account 42's status?", the clerk checks the notepad, then the booklets from newest to oldest, and stops at the first entry. Each booklet has a punched card on its cover that can say "account 42 is definitely not in here" without opening it. At night someone merges a few booklets into one, keeping only the latest entry per account. The analogy breaks at deleting: the office can't cross anything out, so closing an account means writing a "closed" entry, and that entry has to outlive every older booklet that still mentions the account.
in_your_world: You already run LSM trees. Every persistent state store in a Kafka Streams application is a RocksDB instance on the instance's local disk: aggregations write to its memtable, flushes and compactions run in the background, and the memory and I/O you see come from those, tunable through `RocksDBConfigSetter`. Cassandra, which Temporal supports as a persistence store, is one too. In your own schema the question is which shape a table has. An idempotency-key table with random keys, millions of inserts and lookups by exact key is LSM-shaped: in PostgreSQL or Oracle each insert dirties a random index leaf, as the first Try it measured. A ledger read by account and date range is B+tree-shaped, and an LSM tree would have to merge several files for every range.
mistake: The common mistake is treating deletes as free in an LSM store, for example using a Cassandra table as a work queue: insert a row per pending settlement, delete it when it is processed, and read "the oldest pending rows". Every delete writes a tombstone, and a read of the queue's partition must step over all of them until compaction removes them, which in Cassandra waits at least `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days). Cassandra logs a warning when one query reads 1,000 tombstones and fails the query at 100,000 (the `tombstone_warn_threshold` and `tombstone_failure_threshold` defaults). People make the mistake because deletes look like they shrink the data. Design so that deleted data sits in partitions nobody reads again, for example one partition per hour of work, or use a log built for queues, such as a Kafka topic.

compare.title: One random-key insert: B+tree vs LSM tree

a.label: B+tree (PostgreSQL)
a.title: update in place
a.src:
1. descend the index: root and internal page (cached)
2. read the leaf: probably not cached, a random read
3. change the leaf in memory, mark it dirty
4. WAL record; a full page image if this is the
   page's first change since the checkpoint
5. later: write the whole 8 KB page back

write cost: about one page per insert
read cost:  one page per level

b.label: LSM tree (RocksDB)
b.title: write out of place
b.src:
1. append to the WAL
2. insert into the memtable (RAM)
3. later: flush 64 MB of sorted keys in one
   sequential write
4. later: compaction rewrites the key at each
   level it moves through

write cost: a few bytes now, rewritten ~10x later
read cost:  memtable + one file per level, minus
            the files the Bloom filters skip

compare.note: The B+tree pays at write time, a page for each random insert, and in exchange a read is one short descent. The LSM tree makes the write itself almost free and sequential, then pays in the background with compaction, and pays at read time with several places to look. Neither is faster in general; the workload decides.

worked.title: Size the Bloom filters for an idempotency-key store

steps.say: The store will hold 200 million idempotency keys across its SSTables. Start from the target false-positive rate p. The bits per key that give rate p, with the best k, follow from the formula: m/n = -ln(p) / (ln 2)^2.
steps.code:
import kotlin.math.ln

fun bitsPerKey(p: Double) = -ln(p) / (ln(2.0) * ln(2.0))

bitsPerKey(0.01)   // 9.59
bitsPerKey(0.001)  // 14.38

steps.say: Turn bits per key into memory. Filters stay in RAM, so this is a real budget line.
Pick the number of hashes: about 0.69 x bits per key. More hashes cost CPU on every lookup, fewer raise the false-positive rate.
steps.code:
k = 0.69 x 9.59 = 6.6, so 7 hashes for 1%
k = 0.69 x 14.38 = 9.9, so 10 hashes for 0.1%

steps.say: Decide with the read cost. A lookup of a new key (the common case for idempotency checks) must ask every file it can't rule out. With 8 files to check, 1% filters waste 0.08 block reads per lookup instead of 8. Going to 0.1% saves 0.07 reads for 120 MB more RAM. Take 1% unless misses dominate and RAM is cheap.
steps.code:
expected wasted reads = files checked x p
  no filters: 8 x 1.0   = 8
  1%:         8 x 0.01  = 0.08
  0.1%:       8 x 0.001 = 0.008

lab.title: Build an LSM store: memtable, SSTables and Bloom filters
steps: Read the file format at the top of `SSTable.kt`, then `write`, `open` and `entries`: they are done. Read `hash64`, `bitIndex`, `setBit` and `getBit` in `BloomFilter.kt`.
Run the tests once. All 13 fail.
Write `BloomFilter.add` and `mightContain`: split `hash64(key)` into two 32-bit halves and use `bitIndex(h1, h2, i)` for i = 0 until `hashes`. The three `BloomFilterTest` tests pass.
Write `SSTable.get`: filter first, then `blockFor`, then one read of the whole block, then a scan of its records.
Write `LsmStore.put`, `delete`, `get` and `flush`. Remember that `tables` is newest first.
Write `compact`. Run the tests until all 13 pass.
hints: `memtable[key]` returns null both for a tombstone and for a missing key. Use `memtable.containsKey(key)` to tell them apart.

In `SSTable.get`, a block ends at the next block's offset, or at `dataEnd` for the last block. Allocate a `ByteBuffer` of exactly that size and read it with the `readFully` helper: that is the one read the test counts.
While scanning a block, stop as soon as a record's key is greater than the one you want. The records are sorted.
In `compact`, walk `tables.asReversed()` (oldest first) into one `TreeMap`, so newer versions overwrite older ones, then drop the null values before you write.

drill.title: Write the read path and compaction from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Given a `memtable: TreeMap<String, ByteArray?>` (null is a tombstone) and `tables: List<SSTable>` newest first, where `SSTable.get` returns `Value`, `Tombstone` or `Missing`, write `get(key)` and `compact()`. Then answer: why may `compact` drop tombstones here, and when may a real store not?

recap: A B+tree insert of a random key dirties a whole page and, after a checkpoint, logs a full page image. An LSM tree buffers writes in a sorted memtable and writes them out as one sequential file.
An SSTable is an immutable file of records in key order, with a sparse index (the first key of each block) and a Bloom filter, both kept in memory.
A read checks the memtable, then the SSTables newest to oldest, and stops at the first hit. A tombstone means "deleted" and stops the search.
A Bloom filter never says no for a key it holds. With about 10 bits per key and 7 hashes it says a wrong "maybe" about 1% of the time, and it can't help range queries.

Compaction merges files, keeps the newest version of each key, and drops tombstones only when no older file can hold the key. Leveled compaction favours reads and pays more than 10x write amplification; size-tiered favours writes.

quiz.q: A store has four SSTables. You delete `card:7`; its tombstone is in the newest SSTable, and the oldest SSTable still holds `card:7 = ACTIVE`. A compaction merges only the two newest SSTables. May it drop the tombstone?
options: Yes: the tombstone has done its job once it is merged
No: the oldest SSTable still holds card:7, and without the tombstone reads would find ACTIVE again
Yes, but only if the memtable is empty
No: tombstones are never removed from an LSM tree
quiz.why: A tombstone hides older versions of its key. Reads stop at the first table that knows the key, so if the merged file had no entry for card:7, the read would fall through to the oldest file and return ACTIVE: a deleted card comes back. Tombstones are removed once a compaction includes every older file that could hold the key, which is why the last option is wrong.

quiz.q: An SSTable's Bloom filter, sized at 10 bits per key, says "maybe" for `auth:9001`. What do you know?
options: auth:9001 is in the file
auth:9001 is not in the file
auth:9001 is probably in the file; about 1 in 100 keys that are absent also get "maybe", so read the block to be sure
The filter is full and must be rebuilt
quiz.why: A Bloom filter's "no" is certain and its "maybe" is not: all of the key's bits are 1, but other keys may have set them. At 10 bits per key and 7 hashes, about 0.8% of absent keys get a false "maybe". The read goes on to the index and one block, which settles it.

quiz.q: On an LSM store with 6 SSTables, you run a range query: every authorization for card 4242 between 09:00 and 10:00 (keys `card:4242:<time>`). How do the Bloom filters help?
options: They don't: a whole-key filter only answers "is this exact key here?", so the scan opens every file whose key range overlaps
They skip every file that doesn't contain card 4242
They return the keys in the range directly, without reading the files
They halve the number of files, like a binary search
quiz.why: A Bloom filter is built from hashes of whole keys, and hashes destroy order, so it can't say whether any key between two bounds is present. The scan merges every SSTable whose key range overlaps. Prefix filters (RocksDB has them) can help when every query fixes the same key prefix, but a plain whole-key filter can't.

quiz.q: A fraud-scoring service writes 50,000 events a second with random keys and reads back fewer than 100 a second, by exact key. Which compaction style fits, and why?
options: Leveled: it gives the fewest files per read, which matters most here
Size-tiered (or RocksDB's universal compaction): it rewrites each byte fewer times, and reads are rare enough to pay for checking more files
None: an LSM tree can't handle that write rate
Leveled, because size-tiered can't use Bloom filters
quiz.why: The workload is almost all writes, so write amplification is the cost to cut. Size-tiered merges files of similar size and rewrites each byte far fewer times than leveled, which RocksDB says often exceeds 10x. The price is more files per read and more space, and with rare point reads the Bloom filters absorb most of that. Both styles use Bloom filters.

quiz.q: From lesson 4: in the first Try it, 10,000 time-ordered inserts dirtied about 100 pages, and 10,000 random-UUID inserts dirtied about 4,300. Why the difference?
options: Random UUIDs are bigger, so each needs its own page
Ordered keys all go to the rightmost leaf, which fills and splits in turn, while random keys land on leaves all over the index
PostgreSQL compresses ordered keys
The random table had more rows to start with
quiz.why: A B+tree insert goes to the leaf where its key belongs. Ascending keys always belong at the right end, so a few pages take all 10,000 inserts. Random keys belong anywhere, so nearly every insert touches a different one of the index's thousands of leaves. Both UUID kinds are 16 bytes and both tables started with a million rows.

flashcards.front: What is a memtable, and when is it flushed?
flashcards.back: A sorted map in RAM that takes every write. When it reaches a size limit (64 MB by default in RocksDB) it is written out in key order as a new SSTable.

flashcards.front: What makes an SSTable lookup cost one read?
flashcards.back: The sparse index (first key of each block) and the Bloom filter are in memory, so the lookup reads exactly one block, or nothing if the filter says no.

flashcards.front: In what order does an LSM read check its data, and when does it stop?
flashcards.back: Memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest. It stops at the first one that knows the key; a tombstone means "not found".

flashcards.front: Bloom filter: which answer is always right?
flashcards.back: "No". A 0 bit proves the key was never added. "Maybe" can be a false positive.

flashcards.front: How many bits per key for a 1% Bloom filter, and how many hashes?
flashcards.back: About 10 bits per key (RocksDB: 9.9) and k = 0.69 x 10, about 7 hashes.

flashcards.front: When may compaction drop a tombstone?
flashcards.back: Only when no older file left could still hold the key. Cassandra also waits gc_grace_seconds (10 days by default).

flashcards.front: Leveled vs size-tiered compaction in one line each.
flashcards.back: Leveled: at most one file per level per read, write amplification often above 10. Size-tiered: fewer rewrites, more files to read, more temporary space.

terms.plain: A store that buffers writes in a sorted memtable, writes them out as immutable sorted files, and merges those files in the background.
The sorted, in-memory map that takes every write until it is flushed.
Sorted string table: an immutable file of records in key order, with an index and a Bloom filter.
An index with one entry per block (its first key and offset) rather than one per key.
A bit array plus k hash functions that answers "definitely not present" or "maybe present" for a key.
A "maybe" from a Bloom filter for a key that was never added. It costs one wasted read.
Merging SSTables into new ones, keeping the newest version of each key and dropping what it can.
How many disk reads one lookup needs. In an LSM tree it grows with the number of files to check.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why your Kafka Streams state store (RocksDB) can take 50,000 writes a second on one disk while the PostgreSQL table with a random UUID primary key struggles at a few thousand. Explain what each does on a write, and what RocksDB pays for its speed.
explain_back.answer: PostgreSQL keeps the index as a B+tree and changes it in place. Each insert with a random key belongs on a different leaf, so it reads that leaf, dirties the whole 8 KB page, logs a full copy of the page if it is the first change since the checkpoint, and later writes the page back. That is several kilobytes of I/O for a few dozen bytes of data. RocksDB appends the write to its log and puts it in a sorted memtable in memory. When the memtable fills, it writes it out as one sorted file in a single sequential write. The price comes later and elsewhere: compaction rewrites the same data several times as it merges files, often ten times or more with leveled compaction, and a read may have to look in the memtable and several files, newest first. Bloom filters keep most of those extra reads off the disk, but they can't help range scans.

deeper.body:
**Which files make up the database?** Your lab trusts the file names on disk. That breaks if a crash hits in the middle of a compaction, after the new file is written but before the inputs are deleted: on restart both are there, and since the merged file has no entry for a key whose tombstone it dropped, a read falls through to an old input and the deleted value comes back. RocksDB keeps a MANIFEST, a small log of changes to the set of live files: "add these outputs, remove these inputs" is one record, so a compaction takes effect all at once or not at all. Files that the MANIFEST doesn't list are deleted at startup.

**The memtable's own log.** The memtable is lost in a crash, so every write first goes to a WAL. Once a memtable is flushed, its part of the WAL is no longer needed and is deleted. Lesson 6 builds a WAL and the recovery that replays it. Cassandra calls its WAL the commit log.

**Smaller filters, and fewer levels to search.** RocksDB's Ribbon filter (since version 6.15) gives the same false-positive rate in about 30% less space, for 3 to 4 times the CPU time. With `level_compaction_dynamic_level_bytes`, the default since RocksDB 8.4, the level sizes are worked out from the last level, which ends up holding about 90% of the data, so space amplification stays near 1.1.

**Range scans in an LSM tree.** A scan opens an iterator on the memtable and on every SSTable whose key range overlaps, and merges them with a heap, as compaction does, skipping shadowed versions and tombstones. Leveled compaction keeps that to one file per level. This is also where Cassandra's choice to sort by a hash of the partition key shows: ranges only work inside one partition.
